clue.text: Call NE9 to show it's been washed and ironed

indicators.note: the letters are rearranged in order to show something else, a new phrase put on display

blocks.note: the numeral spelt out as a word

explanation.surface: Phone a laundry somewhere in the north-east postcode area to prove the washing is done.
explanation.walkthrough: NE9 looks like a postcode, but the 9 must be spelt out as NINE before the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Linen that has come back laundered and pressed is fresh, so the phrase describes exactly what the clue says.

clue.text: Tendency to write vocal music

blocks.note: to pen a letter is to write it
a chant is sung or intoned music

explanation.surface: Someone with a habit of composing songs.
explanation.definitionFit: A penchant is a strong liking or inclination, a near synonym of a habitual leaning.

clue.text: Commercial opening is coming

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial on TV
a vent is a hole or outlet

explanation.surface: A business is about to open its doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial opening' reads as a shop launch; split it into an advert and a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Advent means an arrival, from Latin adventus, so it is a noun for a coming.

clue.text: Most cruel guys, maybe - don't tangle with them

indicators.note: maybe hints the following letters are only one possible arrangement, so they may be reordered

explanation.surface: A warning to keep clear of the nastiest thugs around.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost a definition in itself: the cruellest guys are exactly the people the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: Ugly customers are dangerous, unpleasant people, the sort anybody sensible avoids getting into a fight with.

clue.text: Lyrics fitted to lyre without Ove Arup's finale

indicators.note: fitted suggests being adjusted or reshaped, so the following words are reworked
without is used in its old sense of outside, so one part wraps round another
a finale is the closing part, so only the end of the word is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the engineer's surname

explanation.surface: Song words set to a lyre, without the ending of the engineer Ove Arup.
explanation.walkthrough: Ove Arup was the engineer behind the Sydney Opera House. The rearranged 'to lyre' sits outside the inserted OVE plus P.
explanation.definitionFit: Romantic verse is a kind of lyric writing, and lyrics are poems meant to be sung or expressing feeling.

clue.text: Burner for body spotted coming up from the range

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a funeral pyre burns a corpse

explanation.surface: A cremation fire glimpsed rising from the mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pyrenees are the mountain range dividing France from Spain, so they are a particular range.

clue.text: Prize, a look back at the dome

indicators.note: back tells us to read the short phrase before it in the other direction

blocks.note: a, plus lo, the old word for look

explanation.surface: A trophy winner glances back at the Millennium Dome.
explanation.walkthrough: Lo, as in 'lo and behold', is a crossword favourite for look.
explanation.definitionFit: A cupola is a small rounded dome on a roof, so it is a type of dome.

clue.text: Say "Go away!" at end of brake

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the exclamation and write down the word that matches its sound

blocks.note: the cry used to scare off a cat or a bird

explanation.surface: Someone shouting at the end of a car brake, or a brake van.
explanation.definitionFit: A brake shoe is the curved block that presses against the wheel, the working part at the business end of a brake.

clue.text: Hides falsehoods - attempt to follow first

indicators.note: first says the word for follow comes before the word for attempt

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them
to have a go is to make an attempt

explanation.surface: Someone conceals untruths and tries to keep on the trail.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie doggo is an informal idiom for staying hidden and keeping quiet, like a dog lying still.

clue.text: Solvers, this is missing in Salad Days

indicators.note: the two letters spelling the little word is go missing from the word just before

blocks.note: the solvers are you, the people reading the clue

explanation.surface: Solvers are told this is absent from the musical Salad Days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This is missing' reads as a comment, but it means THIS with IS removed. Salad Days is a 1950s British musical, and the phrase comes from Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: In Antony and Cleopatra salad days are a person's green, inexperienced early years, so the phrase means youth.

clue.text: Going for gold with a fruit (recipe misplaced)

indicators.note: the letter that abbreviates recipe has been put in the wrong place, so the word's letters are reordered

blocks.note: a cherry is a stone fruit

explanation.surface: An athlete chasing an Olympic medal, with a fruit dish whose recipe has gone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: R stands for recipe, as on a prescription. One R of the fruit moves to sit just after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: The gold is the bullseye of an archery target, so shooting arrows means literally aiming for gold.

clue.text: I agree with gold (apart from mistakes outside) - 16!

indicators.note: apart from, read with outside, says two separated letters stand on either side of the rest
outside places the split pair round the other letters

blocks.note: E is the scorer's abbreviation for an error, twice for the plural

explanation.surface: Someone agreeing to take gold, so long as errors are kept outside.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the 16-across answer, NOT A PRETTY SIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ugly to look at offends the eye, the literal sense of sore to the eyes.

clue.text: Field for good guy with a higher degree than 23 down

blocks.note: a saint is a good person, abbreviated

explanation.surface: A field set aside for a decent fellow with better qualifications than another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degree' looks academic but means degree of comparison: 23 down is LESS, the comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatically the superlative ranks above the comparative, so smallest-amount form outranks the comparative little form.

clue.text: Dumb blonde at Nottingham?

blocks.note: a goose is a silly person

explanation.surface: A slur on a not-too-bright blonde woman from Nottingham.
explanation.walkthrough: Goose Fair is Nottingham's huge annual autumn funfair, once a market for geese.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue points to the famous Nottingham fair, whose name splits into words for silly and blonde.

clue.text: Vegetables on credit at break

indicators.note: in a down clue on means the first word is placed above the second

blocks.note: buying on tick means buying on credit

explanation.surface: Buying vegetables on credit at a break in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: On tick is British slang for on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: A greenstick fracture is an incomplete bone fracture typical of children, so the word names a kind of break.

clue.text: State of Denmark? Nonsense - almost American one

indicators.note: almost says the word is not given in full, its ending being cut short

blocks.note: an American state, following on from State in the clue

explanation.surface: Questioning whether Denmark is a state and dismissing the idea as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's 'Something is rotten in the state of Denmark' supplies the definition; the US state loses its final EE.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's line says Denmark is rotten, so its condition is one of decay and corruption.

clue.text: 4 could be grotty in the past

indicators.note: could be says the following letters might become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Something ugly might once have been called grotty.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 is 4 down, UGLY. Grotty is British slang for shabby or unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is not a pretty sight is a common idiom meaning it looks unpleasant or unattractive.

clue.text: Provide inhabitants for the head without half the wealth

indicators.note: half means only the first part of the word is kept
without in its old sense of outside, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: the pate is the top of the head

explanation.surface: Settling people for a leader who has lost half his riches.
explanation.definitionFit: To populate a place is to fill it with people, which is to supply it with residents.

clue.text: Traveller's ear turns up with internal organ

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means reading the word from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: the liver is an internal organ

explanation.surface: A traveller's ear somehow ends up beside an organ inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemuel Gulliver is the voyager of Swift's Gulliver's Travels, the best-known fictional traveller.

clue.text: Refusal to contribute with 22 down and then down for some 11

definitions.text: with 22 down and then down for some 11

blocks.note: first meaning: what someone says who will give nothing at all

blocks.clueFragment: with 22 down and then down for some 11
blocks.note: second meaning: joined to 22 down and then to 23 down, the title of a novel by an Archer

explanation.surface: Someone declining to donate.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 down is MORE and 23 down is LESS, giving Jeffrey Archer's novel Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less; 'some 11' plays on ARCHERY, that is, Archer.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying you will give no money whatever is a flat refusal, and the phrase also opens the Archer title.

clue.text: Turn to Rome with sham utopian

indicators.note: turn asks the following letters to be turned around into a new order

explanation.surface: A sham idealist converts to the Roman Catholic Church.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the man himself: he stayed loyal to Rome and was executed by Henry VIII.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas More wrote Utopia, which coined the word, so he is the original utopian writer.

clue.text: Setter finds shelter from fight

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as me
the lee is the side sheltered from the wind

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler takes cover from a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: A melee is a confused hand-to-hand scuffle, a disorderly brawl involving many people.

clue.text: Spooner's liquid treatment a shambles still?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words are exchanged

blocks.note: a lotion is a liquid rubbed on the skin, and a mess is a shambles; swap their first sounds

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a spilt skin cream is still a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: Something completely unmoving has no movement at all, so it is still in the sense of stationary.

clue.text: Doctor on-line: it is the opposite of 16

blocks.note: L is an abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: An online doctor describes something as the reverse of an ugly sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 across is NOT A PRETTY SIGHT; a moonlit scene is a romantic and pretty one.
explanation.definitionFit: A landscape lit by the moon is the classic picture of beauty, so it suggests a lovely view rather than an ugly one.

clue.text: See 20
Reluctant Scotsman in Scottish region

blocks.note: Ian is a typical Scottish first name

explanation.surface: An unwilling Scot living in part of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian is the Scottish form of John.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lothians are the area round Edinburgh, historically counties and still a region of Scotland.

clue.text: See 21
Right oven? Cook in it

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for right
an oast is a kiln for drying hops

explanation.surface: Asking if this is the correct oven and telling someone to cook in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Oast houses, with their cowled roofs, are a familiar sight in the hop country of Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast is to cook food with dry heat, typically in an oven, so it is a particular way of cooking.

clue.text: See 4
